rv.q: The result is the funniest new play on Broadway this season.
A slippery, sensitive, clever play about how we reveal ourselves by what we choose to bristle over and what we find funny.
“The Balusters,” which debuts tonight at Manhattan Theatre Club, may be the most vital and timely show on Broadway this season.
The Balusters, as performed by Leon’s very fine ensemble, is an entertaining and well-observed look at the blusters of the privileged few.
Lindsay-Abaire has created a bunch of witheringly annoying and yet highly entertaining characters.
All of these are served in ample proportions in this richly funny if schematic comedy.
Once you lock into the rippling threats, alliances, and power shifts within this clique of homeowners, The Balusters plays out like a series of meetings of the Mafia.

Line by line and moment by moment, “The Balusters” is an engrossing and enjoyable watch, fueled by Lindsay-Abaire’s impolite humor and the cast’s sparky connectivity and willing embrace of the bonkers.
The Balusters is never less than entertaining.
The Balusters feels more like the latter – which makes it both more fun and less resonant than it probably should be.
The Balusters is the best play of the season and the funniest current night out.
A highly clever and comedic script combines with an all-star cast to create a spot-on satire.

Under Kenny Leon’s superb direction, each performer offers up a precise characterization and peerless line deliveries, all of which make this extremely enjoyable show even funnier and more profound than it is on the page.
David Lindsay-Abaire’s fresh and funny comedy uses the pettiness, blind spots and outright biases of the diverse characters who are involved to comment with sharp insight on The Way We Live Now.
Fortunately, David Lindsay-Abaire performs an alchemical feat, transmuting the petty skirmishing, not-so-subtle digs, and brazen power plays into pure hilarity.
Here, the playwright takes a simple conceit and mines it for hilarious social satire featuring a gallery of memorable characters played by a top-flight cast.
Top-notch comedy and covetable home decor—all in a tidy 100-minute package.

Brava and bravo all around for making this social satire an entertaining and often very funny night on the town, especially when we can hide in the audience and watch the fireworks (ranging from sparklers to aerial rockets) going off from a safe distance.
He makes us learn to like these people, with all their blind spots, their self-righteous stands, their manipulations, their passive aggression.
Regardless of anything else, The Balusters is hilarious, skewering not only neighborhood associations but also identity politics while maintaining compassion for all its characters.
Witty and always engaging, though its ham-fistedness might leave you longing for the nuance of Lindsay-Abaire's past triumphs.
The true shining star of the show is undeniably Burke's Penny, serving as the comedic relief that thankfully treads on several tension-filled moments before they venture into beating a dead horse.
Thomas and Rose deliver two completely different performances that make beautiful dissonance.

It’s never easy to reconcile preaching with satire, though, and unfortunately, “Balusters” seems more concerned about reinforcing lessons that will sit comfortably with a Broadway audience than taking a candid look at the issues and conflicts it addresses.
A deliciously barbed comedy where civility crumbles and the laughs land hard.
It is the kind of work I crave in a comedy-- insightful, entertaining, uproariously funny, perspicaciously comments on our time and stays with you long after the curtain comes down.
This year, it appears that one of those marvelous shows is The Balusters.
The Balusters is not just a fabulous new play; it is a vital, invigorating reminder that even the most polite rooms can contain seismic change.
“The Balusters” is a must-see production that accomplishes what the best social comedies do: it makes us laugh at petty squabbles while forcing us to confront the uglier truths underneath.
The real threat to Vernon Point isn't a stop sign—it's the people voting on it. David Lindsay-Abaire's The Balusters is razor-sharp and hits uncomfortably close to home.

The Balusters boasts plenty of curb appeal while delving into the bumptious personalities of a community association in an unnamed city seeking to protect the aesthetics (and resell value) of their historic homes.
A master craftsman who writes witty and neat boulevard comedies that amuse for a couple of hours.
The Balusters provides more gut-busting laughter than any show this season.
This is comedy with teeth, where civility is a costume and hypocrisy is the true language spoken.

cn.t: Lindsay-Abaire's sharp HOA comedy earns mostly positive reviews for its witty skewer of local politics and stellar ensemble cast, though some critics find the premise familiar and the emotional beats underdeveloped.

vr.q: The Balusters might just be my favorite play currently on Broadway.
The zippy pacing and delightful performances make this one a likely crowd-pleaser despite the jokes being a little too on the nose and the messaging being severely heavy-handed.
